sweep_summary: Portuguese (port1283) is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Wetzels 2007. Nothing contradicts the classification. Confirming/refining first-hand statements read: Garcia 2017 Phonology (postprint; weight rule + Houaiss counts; best new statement), Carvalho 1989 (moraic restatement; final /-s/ not heavy), Cantoni 2013 thesis and Cantoni 2008 (three-syllable window, penult default, ASPA type frequencies 67/18/15), Bisol 1994 and Lee 1994 (Letras de Hoje scans, scanned: the original weight rule and the morphological weight-insensitive alternative), Lu et al. 2018 and Frota et al. 2020 (EP: 74% penult / 23% final / 3% antepenult types; window), Guzzo 2018, Guzzo & Garcia 2021, Butler & Frota 2018 (window / penult-most-frequent only); Wetzels 2007 re-downloaded and the catalog quote verified verbatim (p. 32). Secondary-stress papers (Moraes 2003, Arantes & Barbosa 2006, Fernandes-Svartman 2012, Lee 2002, Collischonn 1994) and Santos 2003 / Moraes 2008 are silent on primary placement. Not obtainable: Veiga et al. 2013 (Springer JS challenge; abstract only), Castelo 2005 and Correia 2009 (ULisboa repository timed out), Roca 1999, Vigário 2003, Sandalo 2006, Frota & Vigário 2001 etc. (de Gruyter/Benjamins/JSTOR/SAGE paywalls), Schwindt 2001 and Abaurre & Galves 1998 (SciELO 403), print-only Pereira 1999 (highest acquisition priority: EP book-length metrical analysis), Pereira & Araujo 2007, Walters 1994, Delgado Martins 1982. all discovery went through Semantic Scholar/Crossref APIs, journal archives and repository endpoints. Only an English tesseract model is installed, so the Portuguese scanned quotes are normalised from eng-model output and marked as such.

sources.quote: Primary stress placement in Portuguese non-verbs can be largely explained by weight, in terms of the following generalisations (Bisol 1992): stress is final (U) if the word-final syllable is heavy—where heavy is defined as containing a diphthong, a nasal vowel or a coda consonant (1a)—Portuguese has no long vowels. sources.note: Non-verb stress: final if final syllable heavy (diphthong, nasal vowel, coda), else penultimate; trisyllabic window; Houaiss counts (N=163,625): regular XH́ 14.7% + X́L 57.27% = 72%; irregular XĹ 3.46%, X́H 11.33%, APU 13.05%. sources.quote: NCEs in BP have either penultimate stress (e.g., psíco 'psycho', elétro 'electro', hídro 'hydro') or antepenultimate stress (e.g., hétero 'hetero'). NCE+Dep structures exhibit a single primary stress, which respects the trisyllabic window for stress in BP. Thus, in NCE+Dep, stress will fall on the rightmost element (Dep): psicología.
sources.note: Prosodic-word study of neoclassical compounds; only states the trisyllabic window and that dependent NCE compounds carry one primary stress; no placement rule.

sources.quote: EP has variable stress, similarly to English, Spanish, Catalan, and Hebrew (but unlike French or Finnish). Stress may fall within the last three syllables of the prosodic word and it can distinguish between lexical items (e.g., bambo [ˈbɐ̃bu] / bambu [bɐ̃ˈbu], 'lax' / 'bamboo'; explícito / explicito 'explicit' / 'I make explicit'). ... The frequency of trochaic disyllabic words in EP varies between 66 and 74% in adult speech and 63 and 70% in child-directed speech ... the traditional dominant view in the literature on EP assumes that penultimate stress is the common stress pattern (Viana et al., 1996).
sources.note: Infant perception study; describes EP stress as variable, contrastive, within a three-syllable right-edge window, penultimate most common; no weight rule.

sources.quote: According to the database of Frequency Patterns of Phonological Objects in Portuguese (FrePOP, Frota et al., 2010), 74% of Portuguese words with two or more syllables have penultimate stress, 23% of words have their stress on the final syllable and 3% of words are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable. However, if we consider the token frequency and take monosyllabic words into account, the distributions of penultimate stress and final stress become very close (with final stress above 40%)

sources.quote: O acento lexical, no PB, se restringe a uma janela de três sílabas, ao fim da palavra, formando oxítonas, paroxítonas ou proparoxítonas (cf. BISOL, 1999; CAMARA JÚNIOR, 1970). ... Palavras paroxítonas prevalecem numericamente sobre proparoxítonas e oxítonas ... Bisol (1992, p. 69) apresenta a seguinte regra ... Regra do Acento Primário. Domínio: a palavra. i. Atribua um asterisco (*) à sílaba pesada final, i.e, sílaba de rima ramificada. ii. Argues stress is lexically stored rather than rule-assigned.
